entries.passageText: The LORD bless thee, and keep thee; The LORD make His face to shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee; The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.
entries.reflection: The priestly blessing moves from protection, to grace, to peace, as if peace is where blessing finally arrives. It is spoken over the whole people, not earned by any one person. Wherever you are today, these words have been said over you for generations.
studyPrompts: Which of the blessing's phrases do you most need today?
How might you be a source of shalom for the people you serve with?
Who would you want to bless with these words?

entries.passageText: Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of good courage; be not affrighted, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.’
entries.reflection: Joshua was told to be strong and of good courage as he took up a heavy responsibility. The reason given is not his own strength but that God is with him wherever he goes. That promise travels with you to every posting.
studyPrompts: What responsibility in front of you calls for courage?
How does knowing you are not alone change the way you face it?
Where have you seen strength given to you when you needed it?

entries.passageText: [A Psalm] of David. The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
entries.reflection: David names his fear honestly, then asks a question that shrinks it: whom shall I fear? Light, salvation, stronghold: each image is a place to stand. Fear may remain, but it no longer sets the terms.
studyPrompts: What fear is closest to the surface for you today?
Which image, light, salvation, or stronghold, speaks most to you, and why?
How can you remind yourself of this verse when fear rises?

entries.passageText: And He said: ‘My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest.’
entries.reflection: Moses asked to know the way forward; God answered with presence and rest. Rest here is more than sleep: it is the settledness of not travelling alone. Even on a long day it is possible to rest in that presence.
studyPrompts: Where do you feel restless or unsettled right now?
What does it mean to you that presence comes before rest in this verse?
How might you keep a moment of rest, even a brief one, today?

entries.passageText: It is a good thing to give thanks unto the LORD, And to sing praises unto Thy name, O Most High; To declare Thy lovingkindness in the morning, And Thy faithfulness in the night seasons,
entries.reflection: This psalm, the song for the Sabbath day, pairs morning and night: lovingkindness at the start of the day and faithfulness in the dark. Thanks can frame even a demanding schedule. A brief word of gratitude at waking and at lights-out is a practice anyone can keep.
studyPrompts: What lovingkindness can you name from this morning?
Where have you seen faithfulness in a dark or difficult time?
How could you build a short moment of thanks into the start and end of your day?

entries.passageText: Surely the LORD’S mercies are not consumed, Surely His compassions fail not. They are new every morning; Great is Thy faithfulness.
entries.reflection: These words come from a book of grief, written amid ruin. Hope here is not denial; it is the stubborn noticing that mercy has arrived again this morning. Each new day is evidence that compassion has not run out.
studyPrompts: What loss or disappointment are you carrying right now?
What mercy, however small, can you notice this morning?
How does the idea of mercies 'new every morning' change the way you face tomorrow?

entries.passageText: But they that wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; They shall mount up with wings as eagles; They shall run, and not be weary; They shall walk, and not faint.
entries.reflection: The prophet speaks to people who are worn out. Strength is renewed in stages: soaring, running, and finally walking without fainting. On some days, walking without fainting is victory enough.
studyPrompts: Which stage, soaring, running, or walking, describes you today?
What does 'waiting for the LORD' look like in your daily life?
Where do you need renewed strength this week?

entries.passageText: Thou shalt not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.
entries.reflection: Before the command to love your neighbour comes a harder one: do not take vengeance or bear a grudge. Grudges are heavy to carry in a close-knit unit. Letting one go makes room for the love the verse asks for.
studyPrompts: Is there a grudge you are holding that is weighing on you?
What would it take to set it down?
Who is a 'neighbour' to you in your current setting?

entries.passageText: It hath been told thee, O man, what is good, And what the LORD doth require of thee: Only to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.
entries.reflection: Micah reduces the demands of a good life to three: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. They are simple to say and take a lifetime to practise. Each can be lived out in today's ordinary duties.
studyPrompts: Which of the three, justice, mercy, or humility, comes most naturally to you?
Which is hardest for you right now?
What is one specific way you can act justly today?

entries.passageText: If I take the wings of the morning, And dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; Even there would Thy hand lead me, And Thy right hand would hold me.
entries.reflection: The psalmist imagines going as far as possible, to the wings of the morning and the uttermost parts of the sea, and finds God's hand there too. For anyone at sea or far from home, this is a direct promise. Distance from family is real, but it is not distance from God.
studyPrompts: How far from home do you feel right now?
What would it mean to feel God's hand leading you where you are?
How can you stay connected to the people and community you miss?

entries.passageText: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart, And saveth such as are of a contrite spirit.
entries.reflection: The psalmist says the LORD is near to the broken-hearted. Grief can feel like being cut off from everyone, but this verse places God closest at exactly that moment. You do not have to be whole to be near Him.
studyPrompts: Where does your heart feel broken right now?
What comfort have you found in past times of loss?
Who could you share your grief with?

entries.passageText: Whatsoever thy hand attaineth to do by thy strength, that do; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
entries.reflection: Koheleth urges us to do with all our strength whatever is in our hand to do, because life is limited. Duty done wholeheartedly is a way of honouring the time we are given. Half-effort wastes days we will not get back.
studyPrompts: What task is in your hand today?
Where are you holding back effort?
How does remembering that life is short change how you work?

entries.passageText: and Mizpah, for he said: ‘The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another.
entries.reflection: Laban's words at Mizpah ask the LORD to watch between two people who will be apart. When you cannot watch over the ones you love, you can entrust them to the One who can.
studyPrompts: Who are you apart from right now?
What would you ask God to watch over for them?
How can you stay connected across the distance?

entries.passageText: When pride cometh, then cometh shame; But with the lowly is wisdom.
entries.reflection: Proverbs sets pride and shame side by side, and puts wisdom with the lowly. Humility is not weakness; it is seeing yourself accurately. It keeps you teachable.
studyPrompts: When has pride led you into trouble?
Who do you know who carries their skill humbly?
What could you learn from someone you usually overlook?

entries.passageText: Wait on the LORD; Be strong, and let thy heart take courage; Yea, wait thou for the LORD.
entries.reflection: The psalm repeats its call to wait for the LORD, with strength and courage in between. Waiting is not passive here; it takes a strong heart. Patience is a form of courage.
studyPrompts: What are you waiting for right now?
What helps you keep your heart strong while you wait?
How have past waits turned out?

entries.passageText: Let not kindness and truth forsake thee; Bind them about thy neck, write them upon the table of thy heart;
entries.reflection: Proverbs asks you to bind kindness and truth to yourself and write them on your heart. They are meant to go together: kindness without truth flatters, and truth without kindness wounds. Keep both close.
studyPrompts: Is there someone who needs both truth and kindness from you?
Which one comes more easily to you?
How could you write these on your heart?

entries.passageText: For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you a future and a hope.
entries.reflection: Jeremiah sent these words to exiles far from home, telling them that God had a future and a hope in mind for them. Even a hard posting is not outside God's plans. The purpose may not be clear yet, but it is there.
studyPrompts: Where do you feel far from home or from your purpose?
What hope do you hold for the future?
How can you seek good where you are now?

entries.passageText: They that sow in tears Shall reap in joy. Though he goeth on his way weeping that beareth the measure of seed, He shall come home with joy, bearing his sheaves.
entries.reflection: The psalm pictures someone who goes out weeping, carrying seed, and comes home with joy, carrying a harvest. Time away is often hard, but it is not wasted. Homecoming can bring the fruit of what was sown in tears.
studyPrompts: What have you sown in a hard season?
What are you looking forward to about coming home?
Who will you share your joy with?

entries.passageText: Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry; For anger resteth in the bosom of fools.
entries.reflection: Koheleth warns against being quick to anger. Anger itself may come, but letting it settle in and stay is foolish. Slowing down gives wisdom room to work.
studyPrompts: What makes you quick to anger?
What helps you slow down before reacting?
Is there anger you need to let go of?

entries.passageText: Trust in the LORD with all thy heart, And lean not upon thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge Him, And He will direct thy paths.
entries.reflection: Proverbs asks for trust with the whole heart, not leaning only on your own understanding. Our view is always partial. Trust means acting faithfully even when you cannot see the whole path.
studyPrompts: Where are you leaning only on your own understanding?
What would trusting with your whole heart look like here?
How has a path become clearer for you before?

entries.passageText: Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him that is alone when he falleth, and hath not another to lift him up.
entries.reflection: Koheleth notes that two are better than one, because when one falls the other lifts him up. Service life depends on this truth. No one should have to fall alone.
studyPrompts: Who lifts you up when you fall?
Who might need you to lift them up?
What makes it hard to let others help you?

entries.passageText: He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; And he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
entries.reflection: Proverbs ranks the person who rules their own spirit above the one who takes a city. Self-mastery is harder than outward victory. It is also the strength that holds in pressure.
studyPrompts: Where do you most need to rule your spirit?
What helps you stay calm under pressure?
Who models self-control for you?

entries.passageText: Better is a handful of quietness, Than both the hands full of labour and striving after wind.
entries.reflection: Koheleth says a handful with quiet is better than two hands full of toil and chasing after wind. More is not always better. Contentment is knowing when you have enough.
studyPrompts: What are you chasing that may be wind?
What gives you quiet?
What is enough for you right now?

entries.passageText: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice, And the knowledge of God rather than burnt-offerings.
entries.reflection: Through Hosea, God says He desires mercy rather than sacrifice. Outward observance matters, but it is meant to come with lovingkindness toward others. How we treat people is central.
studyPrompts: Where could you show mercy today?
How do your practices shape the way you treat others?
Who has shown you mercy?

entries.passageText: These are the things that ye shall do: Speak ye every man the truth with his neighbour; execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates;
entries.reflection: Zechariah calls on everyone to speak the truth with their neighbour, and to judge with truth and peace. Truth and peace are linked: honest dealing makes lasting peace possible. Deception may buy quiet, but not peace.
studyPrompts: Is there a truth you need to speak?
How does honesty support peace in your team?
What makes truth-telling hard?

entries.passageText: A Song of Ascents. I will lift up mine eyes unto the mountains: From whence shall my help come? My help cometh from the LORD, Who made heaven and earth.
entries.reflection: The psalmist lifts his eyes to the mountains and asks where help will come from. His answer is the Maker of heaven and earth. When the way ahead is uncertain, he looks up as well as around.
studyPrompts: What is uncertain for you right now?
Where do you look for help first?
What reminds you that you are not alone?

entries.passageText: For the poor shall never cease out of the land; therefore I command thee, saying: ‘Thou shalt surely open thy hand unto thy poor and needy brother, in thy land.’
entries.reflection: The Torah says that there will always be people in need, so the hand must be opened. Generosity is not a one-time act but a habit, because need is ongoing. An open hand starts with an open heart.
studyPrompts: Who in your circle is in need?
What can you give, of time, attention or resources?
What makes your hand close?

entries.passageText: So he shepherded them according to the integrity of his heart; And lead them by the skilfulness of his hands.
entries.reflection: The psalm remembers David, who shepherded his people with an upright heart and skilful hands. Leadership needs both: integrity and competence. One without the other falls short.
studyPrompts: Who leads you with both integrity and skill?
Which of the two do you need to grow in?
How can you care for those in your charge?

entries.passageText: And I heard the voice of the Lord, saying: Whom shall I send, And who will go for us? Then I said: ‘Here am I; send me.’
entries.reflection: Isaiah hears the question, Whom shall I send? and answers, Here am I; send me. Many who serve have made a similar choice. Service begins with being willing to be sent.
studyPrompts: What made you willing to serve?
Where are you being asked to step forward now?
How do you keep that willingness alive?

entries.passageText: And unto man He said: ‘Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; And to depart from evil is understanding.’
entries.reflection: Job concludes that wisdom is reverence for God and understanding is turning from evil. Wisdom is not just cleverness; it is a way of living. It shows in what you choose to avoid as much as what you pursue.
studyPrompts: What does reverence look like in your daily life?
What evil do you need to turn away from?
Who do you consider wise, and why?

entries.passageText: But let justice well up as waters, And righteousness as a mighty stream.
entries.reflection: Amos pictures justice rolling down like waters and righteousness like a mighty stream. It is meant to flow constantly, not trickle. Each fair act adds to the stream.
studyPrompts: Where do you see injustice that troubles you?
What fair act can you take this week?
How do you keep justice flowing in small things?

entries.passageText: So teach us to number our days, That we may get us a heart of wisdom.
entries.reflection: The psalm asks God to teach us to number our days so we gain a heart of wisdom. Remembering that life is limited is not morbid; it sharpens what matters. Each day becomes worth using well.
studyPrompts: How do you feel when you think about the length of life?
What matters most to you when you number your days?
What would you change if you counted each day?

entries.passageText: Behold, I will do a new thing; Now shall it spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, And rivers in the desert.
entries.reflection: Isaiah hears God promise a new thing: a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert. Renewal can begin even in barren places. The question is whether we notice it springing up.
studyPrompts: Where do you feel you are in a wilderness?
What new thing might be beginning in your life?
How can you stay open to renewal?

entries.passageText: 'Let be, and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth.'
entries.reflection: Let be, and know that I am God. In the middle of a psalm about turmoil, the call is to stop and be still. Stillness is not doing nothing; it is making room to know God.
studyPrompts: What would it mean for you to let be today?
When can you find a moment of stillness?
What turmoil do you need to set down?

entries.passageText: He shall not be afraid of evil tidings; His heart is stedfast, trusting in the LORD.
entries.reflection: The psalm describes someone who is not afraid of bad news because their heart is steady, trusting in the LORD. Steadfastness does not mean nothing bad will come. It means bad news does not overturn you.
studyPrompts: What news are you afraid of hearing?
What steadies your heart?
How can you be a steady presence for others?

entries.passageText: Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, And that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? When thou seest the naked, that thou cover him, And that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?
entries.reflection: Isaiah says the fast God desires includes feeding the hungry, sheltering the poor, and not hiding from your own flesh. Compassion is practical. It shows up in bread, shelter and presence.
studyPrompts: Who around you needs practical help?
When have you turned away from someone in need?
What compassionate act can you do this week?

entries.passageText: Let us search and try our ways, And return to the LORD.
entries.reflection: Lamentations calls for searching and testing our ways and then returning to the LORD. Reflection is meant to lead somewhere: back to God and to a better path. It is the heart of teshuvah.
studyPrompts: What would you find if you searched your ways today?
What do you need to return to?
When could you set aside time for reflection?

entries.passageText: For His anger is but for a moment, His favour is for a life-time; weeping may tarry for the night, but joy cometh in the morning.
entries.reflection: The psalm says weeping may stay for the night but joy comes in the morning. Pain is real, but it is not the last word. Joy is promised as surely as morning follows night.
studyPrompts: What has felt like a long night for you?
Where have you seen joy return after sorrow?
What small joy can you notice today?

entries.passageText: Withhold not good from him to whom it is due, When it is in the power of thy hand to do it.
entries.reflection: Proverbs says do not withhold good from those to whom it is due when you are able to do it. Responsibility means acting when the power is in your hand. Delayed good can become good never done.
studyPrompts: What good is in your power to do today?
Who is owed something from you, help or thanks?
What makes you put off doing good?

entries.passageText: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
entries.reflection: Koheleth says there is a season for everything. Service life is full of seasons: training, deployment, homecoming, transition. Each has its own purpose, even when it is hard to see.
studyPrompts: What season are you in right now?
What is the purpose of this season for you?
What are you learning in it?

entries.passageText: Thou wilt surely wear away, both thou, and this people that is with thee; for the thing is too heavy for thee; thou art not able to perform it thyself alone.
entries.reflection: Jethro tells Moses that the load is too heavy for him to carry alone. Even the greatest leader in the Torah needed to share the work. Asking for help is wisdom, not weakness.
studyPrompts: What load are you carrying alone?
Who could share it with you?
What stops you from asking for help?

entries.passageText: And Ruth said: ‘Entreat me not to leave thee, and to return from following after thee; for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God;
entries.reflection: Ruth refuses to leave Naomi, binding her life to her mother-in-law's people and God. Her loyalty is chosen, not owed. It became the start of a new family line.
studyPrompts: Who has been loyal to you when they did not have to be?
Where is your loyalty being tested?
What does it cost you to stay loyal?

entries.passageText: Whoso loveth knowledge loveth correction; But he that is brutish hateth reproof.
entries.reflection: Proverbs says whoever loves knowledge loves correction. Discipline and feedback are not insults; they are how we grow. Resisting them keeps us where we are.
studyPrompts: How do you respond to correction?
What feedback have you received recently?
What discipline is helping you grow?

entries.passageText: And the LORD came, and stood, and called as at other times: ‘Samuel, Samuel.’ Then Samuel said: ‘Speak; for Thy servant heareth.’
entries.reflection: When young Samuel finally recognises the call, he answers, Speak; for Thy servant heareth. Listening starts with readiness to hear. It may take more than one call before we understand.
studyPrompts: What might God, or someone near you, be trying to tell you?
What helps you listen well?
Who do you need to listen to more closely?

entries.passageText: A soft answer turneth away wrath; But a grievous word stirreth up anger.
entries.reflection: Proverbs says a soft answer turns away wrath, while a harsh word stirs up anger. Gentleness in speech is a practical skill. It can calm a tense moment before it gets worse.
studyPrompts: When has a gentle word calmed a situation for you?
Where do you tend to answer harshly?
How could you soften one conversation this week?

entries.passageText: He giveth power to the faint; And to him that hath no might He increaseth strength.
entries.reflection: The prophet says God gives power to the faint and increases the strength of those who have none. Strength does not only belong to the strong. It can be given to anyone who is running low.
studyPrompts: Where do you feel faint right now?
Where do you look for strength?
When have you been given strength you did not have?

entries.passageText: There are friends that one hath to his own hurt; But there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
entries.reflection: Proverbs notes that some companions do harm, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother. Not every acquaintance is a friend. A true friend is worth more than many companions.
studyPrompts: Who is a friend who sticks close to you?
Are there companions who bring you harm?
How can you be that kind of friend?

entries.passageText: I wait for the LORD, my soul doth wait, and in His word do I hope. My soul waiteth for the Lord, more than watchmen for the morning; yea, more than watchmen for the morning.
entries.reflection: The psalmist waits for God more than watchmen wait for the morning. Anyone who has stood night watch knows how long that wait can feel. Hope keeps you watching until the light comes.
studyPrompts: What are you waiting for?
What keeps your hope alive during long waits?
What does your night watch look like right now?

entries.passageText: Pleasant words are as a honeycomb, Sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.
entries.reflection: Proverbs compares pleasant words to a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the body. Kind words do real good. They cost nothing and can heal.
studyPrompts: What kind words have stayed with you?
Whom could your words heal today?
What words do you need to stop saying?

entries.passageText: For I have satiated the weary soul, And every pining soul have I replenished.
entries.reflection: God promises, through Jeremiah, to refresh the weary soul and replenish every languishing one. Weariness is not the end. Rest and renewal are promised.
studyPrompts: What has worn you out lately?
What refreshes you?
How could you make room for rest this week?

entries.passageText: As far as the east is from the west, So far hath He removed our transgressions from us.
entries.reflection: The psalmist says God removes our transgressions as far as the east is from the west. That is a distance that never closes. Teshuvah, returning, is always possible.
studyPrompts: What do you need to leave behind?
What makes it hard to accept forgiveness?
Who might you need to forgive?

entries.passageText: A Song of Ascents; of David. LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty; Neither do I exercise myself in things too great, or in things too wonderful for me. Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul; Like a weaned child with his mother; My soul is with me like a weaned child.
entries.reflection: The psalmist says he does not reach for things too great for him; he has calmed and quieted his soul like a weaned child. Simplicity is a kind of peace. It does not need to hold everything.
studyPrompts: What are you reaching for that may be too great?
What helps quiet your soul?
What could you let go of?

entries.passageText: Go to the ant, thou sluggard; Consider her ways, and be wise;
entries.reflection: Proverbs sends the sluggard to learn from the ant. The ant works steadily, without being driven, and is ready when the season turns. There is wisdom in diligence.
studyPrompts: What could you learn from the ant?
Where are you tempted to put things off?
What steady work would prepare you for what is ahead?

entries.passageText: Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and thou shalt fear thy God: I am the LORD.
entries.reflection: The Torah commands rising before the aged and honoring the elderly, and ties it to reverence for God. Respect for elders is part of holiness. Experience deserves honor.
studyPrompts: Who are the elders in your life?
What have you learned from them?
How could you show them respect?

entries.passageText: Cause me to hear Thy lovingkindness in the morning, For in Thee do I trust; Cause me to know the way wherein I should walk, For unto Thee have I lifted up my soul.
entries.reflection: The psalmist asks to hear God's lovingkindness in the morning and to be shown the way to walk. Each morning is a chance to start again with trust. Ask for direction before the day begins.
studyPrompts: How do you start your mornings?
What direction do you need today?
What would hearing kindness in the morning mean to you?

entries.passageText: I lay me down, and I sleep; I awake, for the LORD sustaineth me.
entries.reflection: The psalmist lies down, sleeps and wakes again because God sustains him. Sleep is an act of trust. The tradition's bedtime prayer, Shema al hamitah, offers a similar handing over at the end of the day.
studyPrompts: What makes it hard to lie down in peace?
What would you hand over to God tonight?
What helps you sleep well?

entries.passageText: Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; Save me, and I shall be saved; For Thou art my praise.
entries.reflection: Jeremiah prays, heal me and I shall be healed. Asking for healing is part of prayer; the Amidah's blessing for healing echoes these words. Seeking help from healers is part of that too.
studyPrompts: What healing do you need?
Whom could you ask for help?
Whom could you pray for today?

entries.passageText: I acknowledged my sin unto Thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid; I said: 'I will make confession concerning my transgressions unto the LORD' — And Thou, Thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah
entries.reflection: The psalmist acknowledged his sin, stopped hiding it, and found forgiveness. Hiding guilt makes it heavier. Confession, vidui, opens the way to relief.
studyPrompts: What are you hiding?
What would it mean to acknowledge it?
Whom might you need to make amends to?

entries.passageText: Be strong, and let your heart take courage, All ye that wait for the LORD.
entries.reflection: The psalmist tells all who wait for God to be strong and let their hearts take courage. Encouragement is something we can say to each other, and to ourselves.
studyPrompts: Who needs to hear be strong from you?
What gives your heart courage?
When has someone's encouragement made a difference?

entries.passageText: A Song of Ascents; of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is For brethren to dwell together in unity!
entries.reflection: How good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity. Unity is not just useful; the psalmist calls it good and pleasant. It is worth working for.
studyPrompts: Where do you experience unity?
What threatens unity around you?
What could you do to build it?

entries.passageText: Depart from evil, and do good; Seek peace, and pursue it.
entries.reflection: The psalmist says to seek peace and pursue it. Peace does not happen on its own; it has to be pursued. The sages held up Aaron as one who loved and pursued peace.
studyPrompts: Where is peace needed around you?
What would it mean to pursue it?
What gets in the way of peace for you?

entries.passageText: Love ye therefore the stranger; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.
entries.reflection: The Torah commands loving the stranger, because you were strangers in Egypt. Memory of being an outsider shapes how we treat outsiders. Welcome is a duty.
studyPrompts: When have you felt like a stranger?
Who is a stranger around you now?
How could you welcome them?

entries.passageText: Honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
entries.reflection: Honor your father and your mother is one of the Ten Commandments. Honoring parents continues even when we are far from home. It can look like a call, a letter, or living in a way that honors them.
studyPrompts: How do you honor your parents or those who raised you?
What is hard about it?
What could you do this week to honor your family?

entries.passageText: Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can the floods drown it; If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, He would utterly be contemned.
entries.reflection: Song of Songs says many waters cannot quench love, nor floods drown it. Real love is not for sale. It survives distance and hardship.
studyPrompts: What love has survived distance in your life?
What threatens the love you have?
How could you nurture it today?

entries.passageText: A tranquil heart is the life of the flesh; But envy is the rottenness of the bones.
entries.reflection: Proverbs says a tranquil heart gives life, but envy rots the bones. Envy harms the one who carries it. Contentment is healthier.
studyPrompts: Whom do you envy?
What would a tranquil heart look like for you?
What are you thankful for that you already have?

entries.passageText: When my cares are many within me, Thy comforts delight my soul.
entries.reflection: When cares multiply within the psalmist, God's comforts delight his soul. Worry is real, but it is not the only thing in the heart. Comfort can come alongside it.
studyPrompts: What cares are multiplying for you?
Where do you find comfort?
What comforts could you take time for today?

entries.passageText: When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee, And through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee; When thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned, Neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.
entries.reflection: God promises to be with Israel through waters and fire. The promise is not that hardship will not come, but that God will be present in it.
studyPrompts: What waters or fire are you passing through?
Where have you felt God's presence in hard times?
Who walks through hardship with you?

entries.passageText: If thou doest well, shall it not be lifted up? and if thou doest not well, sin coucheth at the door; and unto thee is its desire, but thou mayest rule over it.’
entries.reflection: God tells Cain that sin crouches at the door and desires him, but he can rule over it. Temptation is real, but it can be mastered. The choice remains yours.
studyPrompts: What crouches at your door?
What helps you master it?
Who could help you?

entries.passageText: And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land unto all the inhabitants thereof; it shall be a jubilee unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family.
entries.reflection: Proclaim liberty throughout the land; these words of the Torah are inscribed on the Liberty Bell. Freedom in the Torah is tied to a return to family and home. Service members know freedom is worth guarding.
studyPrompts: What does freedom mean to you?
What freedom are you serving to protect?
Who is waiting for your return home?

entries.passageText: A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, And loving favour rather than silver and gold.
entries.reflection: Proverbs says a good name is better than great riches. Reputation is built over years and can be lost in a moment. Honor is worth more than gain.
studyPrompts: What kind of name are you building?
What might tempt you to trade it?
Whose good name do you admire?

entries.passageText: When a man voweth a vow unto the LORD, or sweareth an oath to bind his soul with a bond, he shall not break his word; he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth.
entries.reflection: The Torah says that one who makes a vow must not break his word, but do all that he said. Words are binding. Speak carefully and keep what you say.
studyPrompts: Is there a promise you need to keep?
Do you promise too quickly?
What does keeping your word say about you?

entries.passageText: Learn to do well; Seek justice, relieve the oppressed, Judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.
entries.reflection: Isaiah says learn to do good: seek justice, relieve the oppressed, defend the orphan and the widow. Doing good is learned and practiced. It reaches toward the vulnerable.
studyPrompts: What good could you learn to do?
Who is vulnerable around you?
What act of justice is within your reach?

entries.passageText: And if thou draw out thy soul to the hungry, And satisfy the afflicted soul; Then shall thy light rise in darkness, And thy gloom be as the noon-day;
entries.reflection: Isaiah says that if you draw out your soul to the hungry, your light will rise in darkness. Giving yourself to others brings light, to them and to you.
studyPrompts: Who is hungry, in any sense, around you?
What could you give of yourself?
When has giving brought light to you?

entries.passageText: Thy lovingkindness, O LORD, is in the heavens; Thy faithfulness reacheth unto the skies.
entries.reflection: The psalmist says God's lovingkindness reaches the heavens and his faithfulness the skies. God's faithfulness is vast. We can try to reflect it in our own steadiness.
studyPrompts: Where have you seen God's faithfulness?
Where can you be more faithful?
Who has been faithful to you?

entries.passageText: Even a child is known by his doings, whether his work be pure, and whether it be right.
entries.reflection: Proverbs says even a child is known by his doings. Character shows in actions, not in claims. What you do reveals who you are.
studyPrompts: What do your actions say about you?
What would you like them to say?
What action could you take today that reflects your values?

entries.passageText: This is the day which the LORD hath made; We will rejoice and be glad in it.
entries.reflection: This is the day the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it. Today is the day you have. It is a gift, not just a stretch to get through.
studyPrompts: What could you rejoice in today?
How do you want to use this day?
What day are you waiting for, and what about today?

entries.passageText: Take fast hold of instruction, let her not go; Keep her, for she is thy life.
entries.reflection: Proverbs says hold on to instruction and do not let go, for it is your life. Learning is not a phase but a lifelong commitment. Torah study is a lifelong practice in Jewish life.
studyPrompts: What instruction are you holding on to?
What do you want to learn next?
Who teaches you?

entries.passageText: When I behold Thy heavens, the work of Thy fingers, The moon and the stars, which Thou hast established; What is man, that Thou art mindful of him? And the son of man, that Thou thinkest of him?
entries.reflection: Looking at the heavens, the moon and the stars, the psalmist asks: what is man, that You are mindful of him? Creation makes us feel small and also cared for.
studyPrompts: When have you felt small looking at the sky?
What does it mean to you that God is mindful of you?
Where could you notice creation today?

entries.passageText: Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy; Though I am fallen, I shall arise; Though I sit in darkness, the LORD is a light unto me.
entries.reflection: Micah says: though I have fallen, I shall rise; though I sit in darkness, the LORD is a light to me. Falling is not the end. There is light even in darkness.
studyPrompts: Where do you feel you have fallen?
What would rising look like?
What light do you see in your darkness?

entries.passageText: Blessed be the Lord, day by day He beareth our burden, Even the God who is our salvation. Selah
entries.reflection: The psalmist blesses God who bears our burden day by day. Burdens are carried daily, and so is help. You do not carry everything alone.
studyPrompts: What burden are you carrying today?
Who helps carry it?
Whose burden could you help with?

entries.passageText: For My thoughts are not your thoughts, Neither are your ways My ways, saith the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, So are My ways higher than your ways, And My thoughts than your thoughts.
entries.reflection: God says, through Isaiah, my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor my ways your ways. Our view is limited. Humility about what we cannot see is a kind of perspective.
studyPrompts: What are you trying to understand right now?
What might you be missing?
How does a larger view change things?

entries.passageText: and after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire; and after the fire a still small voice.
entries.reflection: Elijah found God not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in a still small voice. The most important things can be quiet. Listen for the small.
studyPrompts: What still small voice might you be missing?
Where do you find quiet?
What small thing deserves more attention?

entries.passageText: God maketh the solitary to dwell in a house; He bringeth out the prisoners into prosperity; The rebellious dwell but in a parched land.
entries.reflection: The psalmist says God sets the solitary in a home. Loneliness is not meant to be permanent. Belonging is part of what God gives.
studyPrompts: When have you felt solitary?
Where have you found a home among people?
Whom could you help belong?

entries.passageText: For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then will relief and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place, but thou and thy father’s house will perish; and who knoweth whether thou art not come to royal estate for such a time as this?’
entries.reflection: Mordecai tells Esther that silence is not neutral, and asks: who knows whether you came to your position for such a time as this? Moral courage means speaking when it matters, even at risk.
studyPrompts: Where might you be called to speak up?
What makes silence tempting?
What position have you been given, and why might it matter?

entries.passageText: Thine own friend, and thy father’s friend, forsake not; Neither go into thy brother’s house in the day of thy calamity; Better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off.
entries.reflection: Proverbs says a neighbor who is near is better than a brother far away. For service members far from home, the people nearby become family. Be that neighbor.
studyPrompts: Who is your near neighbor right now?
How have neighbors helped you?
How could you be a good neighbor this week?

entries.passageText: A merry heart is a good medicine; But a broken spirit drieth the bones.
entries.reflection: Proverbs says a merry heart is good medicine, but a broken spirit dries the bones. Mood and health are linked. Caring for your spirit helps your body.
studyPrompts: What lifts your heart?
Is your spirit feeling broken right now?
Who could you reach out to for support?

entries.passageText: Remove far from me falsehood and lies; Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with mine allotted bread; Lest I be full, and deny, and say: ‘Who is the LORD?’ Or lest I be poor, and steal, And profane the name of my God.
entries.reflection: Proverbs asks for neither poverty nor riches, just enough. Too much can make us forget God; too little can tempt us to wrong. Enough is a gift.
studyPrompts: What is enough for you?
How does money affect your choices?
What would contentment with enough look like?

entries.passageText: For he shall never be moved; The righteous shall be had in everlasting remembrance.
entries.reflection: The psalmist says the righteous will be remembered forever. Jewish tradition keeps memory alive through Yizkor and the yahrzeit. Remembering the good is a way of honoring them.
studyPrompts: Whom do you remember?
How do you keep their memory alive?
What good from their life do you carry?

entries.passageText: And the LORD said unto Moses: ‘Take thee Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is spirit, and lay thy hand upon him; and set him before Eleazar the priest, and before all the congregation; and give him a charge in their sight. And thou shalt put of thy honour upon him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may hearken.
entries.reflection: God tells Moses to lay his hand on Joshua and give him some of his authority before the people. Good leaders prepare the next leaders. Passing on responsibility is part of leadership.
studyPrompts: Who prepared you for your role?
Whom are you preparing?
What authority or knowledge could you share?

entries.passageText: The LORD shall guard thy going out and thy coming in, From this time forth and for ever.
entries.reflection: The LORD shall guard your going out and your coming in, from this time and forever. Wherever the road leads, you are not unguarded. Go out with this blessing.
studyPrompts: Where is your road taking you next?
What blessing do you need for the journey?
Whom would you give this blessing to?
